..
Issued at 227 AM EDT Sat Sep 26 2026

Pattern / Forecast Synopsis: 

Rex block and associated surface high pressure retrograding 
overhead, and to remain in place through the weekend into next week. 
As such, dry and ever so progressively warmer daytime highs into the 
70s, and modest diurnal swings will lead to cooler nighttime lows 
in the 40s and lower 50s for most. 

Meanwhile, vintage El Nino coded longwave troughing currently 
setting up shop across the Pacific Coast will lead to a potent 
return flow of tropical Pacific moisture within an active 
subtropical jet into the Four Corners region, with tropically 
influenced shortwaves ejecting into the southern Plains. Much of 
this moisture to be suppressed to our south by a combination of both 
the rex blocking overhead and a rather unimpressive northern stream 
wave pattern through midweek... until a more potent northern stream 
wave zips into the upper Midwest and brings just enough of a draw of 
the deeper moisture northward into the region to perhaps introduce 
some scattered rain chances around midweek. 

Details: 

Will continue to contend with some fog across the region through the 
morning... and perhaps some localized frost potential in the colder 
interior locales that manage to bottom out near / below 35 degrees. 
Much of this to scour out through early morning, with a warm and 
sunny afternoon resulting as highs top out generally 68 to 75 
degrees amid light NE flow. Another cool night tonight with temps 
perhaps dipping into the upper 30s in colder interior locales, but 
most other places probably wind up anywhere from the low-mid 40s, 
perhaps low 50s along the immediate lakeshores. Current thinking is 
that frost potential will be muted tonight, perhaps occurring on a 
localized scale across the interior cold spots. Warmer days ahead 
Monday and Tuesday with highs perhaps making a run into the upper 
70s in places. Should be noted average highs this time of year are 
generally 61 to 68 degrees. 

Aforementioned Pacific moisture plume to really struggle reaching 
into the region until the middle or end of next week, and 
considering the fickle nature of systems, I remain more pessimistic 
than optimistic in regard to us realizing an appreciable amount of 
rainfall from this feature. Largely split flow should limit the 
northern jet stream's influence in drawing this moisture northward 
into our neck of the woods, but a continued active subtropical jet 
should produce wave after wave of convection and tropical downpours 
across the Four Corners into the southern Plains, leaking into the 
central Plains by early next week (Arizona, New Mexico, Texas, 
Oklahoma, Colorado, and Kansas certainly look to see the brunt of 
these rains, amounting well in excess of 7" in places, and I would 
be unsurprised to see amounts winding up well higher than that 
across TX and OK). More potent northern stream feature to pass into 
the upper Midwest Tuesday into Wednesday, which should finally aid 
enough in drawing that deeper moisture northward. Anticipation is 
that continued southern / central Plains activity will bottle the 
best moisture pooling across that region, while just some scraps of 
moisture get ingested by the aforementioned northern stream wave. 

Timing of this feature's passage through the Great Lakes and 
northern Michigan will dictate whether or not this is a meaningful, 
convectively charged and appreciable amount of rain during the day / 
evening, or a whimpering drizzly disappointment of a rain that 
passes through at night and accomplishes nothing much more than 
annoying everybody with uncomfortable amounts of humidity 
(clearly I'm not emotionally biased). That all being said, 
guidance seems to highlight the Wednesday - Wednesday night 
timeframe to favor best rain chances. Certainly a lot of 
different factors to consider with this pattern's evolution, so 
won't be overly aggressive in rainfall messaging aside from 
mentioning "shower chances" at this juncture... because if this 
feature loses its convective elements with a nighttime passage, 
any stratiform rain will have a boatload of drier air to 
overcome, and top-down saturation processes will be a tall task 
without a deeper moisture surge.
